video_title: Inside the Race to Measure Frontier Intelligence
gist: Ryan, co-founder of third-party AI evaluation firm Vals AI, and a16z's Ben Horowitz argue that independent, held-out benchmarks are becoming the audit layer of the AI economy: public benchmarks are hackable and saturated (Meta's Llama 4 topped public benchmarks while underperforming on Vals' private ones), so labs need credible third-party proof to justify multi-billion-dollar model capex and enterprises need it to justify token spend that is starting to eclipse payroll. The conversation delivers hard token-economics data (Vals burned ~$1.5M of tokens in one month, 10x its salary spend; a Fortune 10 firm rations Claude Code at $100-$300/day per engineer), counterintuitive model-selection findings (Sonnet often costs more than Opus because it is token-hungry; Cognition's Devin is unusually token-efficient), and a policy thesis that government should set rules while private evaluators test whether models can be made to break them.

themes.theme: Independent evals as the AI audit layer

insights.claim: Meta's Llama 4 showed incredible capability on major public benchmarks whose questions and rubrics are open source, while simultaneously underperforming on Vals AI's held-out private benchmarks — direct evidence that self-reported public benchmark scores can diverge sharply from independent measurement.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Treat lab-published benchmark scores as marketing until a third party with held-out sets confirms them; divergence between public and private benchmark results is an early tell on a model release that will disappoint in production.
insights.quote: on our heldout private benchmarks the model is actually underperforming but on all of the the major public benchmarks where that the questions and rubrics are actually open source um it was it was showing incredible capability

insights.claim: Frontier labs themselves want an independent evaluation ecosystem because they need a 'rational buying market' — substantive third-party evidence that a multi-billion-dollar training run produced real capability gains, rather than purely self-reported claims, with Demis Hassabis among those publicly calling for third-party evaluators.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Demand for independent eval is pulled by the sellers, not just imposed by regulators — a structurally durable market that grows with training capex rather than shrinking under lab pushback.
insights.quote: they would like to see that when they invest billions of dollars to build a new model, they're actually substantive ways they can point to evidence

insights.claim: The emergence of a trillion-dollar industry reliably creates demand for an independent testing group, and AI's speed is compressing that pattern — the relevant comparables are rating agencies and audit firms, with the evaluator sitting on both sides of the market (labs proving capability, enterprises choosing adoption strategy).
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frames AI evaluation as a two-sided infrastructure business with recurring revenue from both model builders and buyers — a category where a first credible incumbent can compound trust as Moody's or the Big Four did.
insights.quote: every time a new trillion dollar uh industry emerges um there there there's a need for this independent testing group

insights.claim: Vals AI made an early decision never to sell training data to labs despite being repeatedly pushed to, because combining data sales with evaluation reproduces the Enron conflict-of-interest structure and degrades into 'pay to win the benchmark' — while much of the data-labeling industry now builds gimmick-style benchmarks specifically as a go-to-market for selling data.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: A cleanly stated diligence test for the eval/data-labeling sector: any vendor that both sells training data and publishes benchmarks carries structural credibility risk, which is where the auditing industry's historical blowups came from.
insights.quote: it just becomes pay to pass the audit or or in this case pay to to win the benchmark

insights.claim: Building generation systems and building evaluation methods are tightly coupled — one of the single biggest drivers of model capability is the arrival of a new legible way to evaluate models, so eval innovation is an input to capability progress rather than a downstream scorekeeping function.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Watch new benchmark releases as leading indicators of where the next capability jump will land — labs hill-climb whatever becomes measurable, so the eval defines the next frontier.
insights.quote: one of the biggest drivers for model capability is having a new legible way to evaluate models

themes.theme: Benchmark half-life and the shift to agentic evals

insights.claim: Vals AI deliberately deprecates saturated benchmarks rather than continuing to publish them, on the view that an evaluator's job is to perpetually construct the next mountains for labs to summit — an explicitly infinite game captured in the firm's motto 'always a higher peak'.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Benchmarks have a short commercial half-life, so eval businesses are judged on rate of new benchmark creation, not on catalog size; and any vendor still citing a saturated benchmark is signaling weakness.
insights.quote: in so far as foundation model labs are hill climbing, they're searching for the next peaks to summit. It is our job to perpetually construct these next mountains for them to summit.

insights.claim: Evaluation is structurally inverting: where ImageNet had millions of inputs with a one-to-one image-to-label mapping, modern benchmarks have far fewer tasks (e.g. 'generate me 50 full-stack web applications') paired with a much larger and more complex rubric for grading each output, and this trend will continue as workflows get more complex.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: The cost and defensibility of evals is migrating from data volume to rubric quality and grading infrastructure — favoring firms with domain expertise over firms with large labeling workforces.
insights.quote: generate me 50 fullstack web applications but a much larger complex mechanism for evaluating the output produced

insights.claim: Agentic evaluation now requires testing models running continuously over hours, days, and sometimes weeks, forcing eval infrastructure to support resuming from an individual failed request rather than rerunning the entire trajectory.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Long-horizon agent reliability is now an infrastructure problem in its own right; the same checkpoint/retry requirements apply to enterprises deploying multi-day background agents, creating a tooling market.

insights.claim: Independent evaluators now work inside a roughly six-hour pre-release window before a frontier model drops, running tens of billions of tokens at maximum available rate limits in a massively distributed way so that third-party scores never lag the launch.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Day-one independent scores now land alongside launches, so the market-moving benchmark verdict on a new frontier model arrives within hours rather than weeks — compressing the window for narrative-driven repricing.
insights.quote: we never want to be um kind of a lagging indicator or a delay to a model release

insights.claim: Measuring model intelligence will remain necessarily fuzzy and will be settled by evolving social norms rather than a definitive test — an MPAA-style 'I know it when I see it' regime — whereas today's open benchmarks that certify a level for solving one specific problem are both hackable and too narrow.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz
insights.so_what: Argues against expecting a single canonical AI intelligence score to emerge; value accrues to whoever's norms and rubrics get adopted by the people running companies and finance, not to whoever tops a leaderboard.
insights.quote: I I know it when I see it and I think that um this one I I just think it's going to be necessarily fuzzy but there will develop norms over time

insights.claim: The long-term bottleneck on AI evaluation is not model capability but the ability to take companies' actual work and make it legible — there is no clear test distinguishing an associate from a partner at a law firm, so those distinctions must be made explicit before models can be tested against them.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Identifies workflow codification, not compute or data, as the gating factor on enterprise AI adoption — the firms and vendors that instrument their own work first will adopt fastest.
insights.quote: long term that will be actually the biggest bottleneck, our ability to take companies and their emails and and make them legible

insights.claim: Coding is the leading indicator for every other knowledge-work domain: a model that is a very good coding agent is likely also capable of building PowerPoint slides and DCFs in Excel, so primitives established in code evaluation carry over to other industries.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Coding-agent benchmark progress is a forward read on disruption timing for finance, consulting and other document-heavy knowledge work — watch codegen leaderboards as a proxy for those markets.
insights.quote: coding is a sign for what's to come in every domain

insights.claim: Vals AI's most-used benchmarks target economically meaningful applications — a finance agent benchmark used by a number of large financial institutions to track model improvement, and a vibe-code benchmark measuring whether models can turn a natural language prompt into a full-stack web application, which has tracked model gains over the last nine months.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Large financial institutions are already outsourcing model-selection evidence to a third party, indicating institutional AI procurement is professionalizing into a measurable, auditable process.

insights.claim: A Fortune 10 company rations Claude Code at roughly $100 per engineer per day (recently raised to $300), and because the rate limit resets at 4 p.m. the most productive hours of the workday have shifted to 4-6 p.m., with a dead period in the afternoon when engineers go on walks or get coffee.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that token budgets now dictate large-enterprise work rhythms — and that per-seat AI spend at the high end is already approaching an employee's salary in tokens, a demand signal for inference capacity.
insights.quote: there's a a rate limit which resets at 4 p.m. And so so the most productive hours of work are actually now 4 to 6 p.m. uh when the rate limits reset.

insights.claim: Intelligence is mispriced at every layer of the stack simultaneously: engineers do not know how to apportion a $100 daily budget for maximum productivity, the Fortune 10 employer set that cap arbitrarily because the right level is hard to quantify, and Anthropic runs on pretty narrow margins with massive costs to serve those models.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Pricing for AI labor is unanchored in both directions — expect volatile enterprise budgets and repricing of inference contracts as ROI measurement matures; margin compression risk sits with the model providers.
insights.quote: there is a misvaling of intelligence happening at every layer of the stack

insights.claim: Token spend may start to eclipse salary spend as an enterprise cost line, which forces companies to justify AI ROI far more rigorously than they have over the last six months, making the ability to make internal evals legible the determinant of which company beats its competitors.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Predicts a coming enterprise AI spend audit cycle — a near-term risk to unmeasured seat-based AI revenue and a tailwind for eval, observability and cost-attribution tooling.
insights.quote: a firm really is just its eval

insights.claim: In a one-month uncapped 'token maxing' experiment at Vals AI, engineers averaged one to two billion tokens per day with a peak of six billion tokens by a single engineer in one day, totaling roughly $1.5 million of tokens — about 10x the company's employee salary spend for that month, not a 50/50 split.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Hard upper-bound datapoint on unconstrained AI-native engineering consumption: demand for inference is effectively unbounded at zero marginal price, supporting the compute buildout thesis while underscoring that list-price economics are unworkable for buyers.
insights.quote: it was actually 10x more we were spending in tokens than employee salary for that month

insights.claim: Anthropic's Sonnet is in many cases more expensive to run than Opus because it is so token hungry, so the common heuristic of defaulting to the cheaper model where it seems applicable can end up costing more than using the frontier model.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Per-token price is a misleading proxy for total cost; token efficiency per completed task is the real metric, which changes model-mix economics and undercuts simple 'cheap model tiering' cost strategies.
insights.quote: we're actually seeing in a lot of cases sonnet is more expensive than opus because it is so token hungry

insights.claim: It remains genuinely unclear whether the best OpenAI model or the best Anthropic model will perform better on a given company's repository, with many non-intuitive results, and the middle of the market has grown more complex with multiple tiers per lab plus a growing ecosystem of self-hostable open-source models.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: There is no durable single winner in coding models at the buyer level; switching costs stay low and per-workload evaluation becomes the procurement norm, which caps any one lab's pricing power.
insights.quote: we've seen a lot of non-intuitive examples where you actually had to run the eval to figure out what's going to be the frontier performance for that repository

insights.claim: Vals AI has productized this as Val Smith, which lets any company turn its own GitHub codebase into an internal coding benchmark to find the Pareto-optimal coding agent for its repo — targeting codegen because it is the highest-spend area in enterprise AI.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Private, repo-specific benchmarking is emerging as the enterprise procurement layer for coding agents; the most sophisticated enterprises are already doing it, so expect the market to rationalize away from brand-led model buying.

insights.claim: Vals AI found Cognition's Devin to be notably token efficient and has adopted it more as a result, and found that subscription-based pricing often beats token-based pricing — internally it gives every engineer access to all tools but auto-generates a recommendation for where to start each GitHub issue so usage titrates to the intelligence the task requires.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Token efficiency and pricing model — not raw capability — are becoming the deciding purchase criteria for coding agents, favoring vendors on subscription plans and harnesses that minimize token burn.
insights.quote: the Cognition Devon tool is actually very token efficient and so that's a place we we've chosen to adopt more

insights.claim: OpenRouter — which Stripe just acquired per the host — is better understood as a model gateway than a router, because most usage has the customer choosing the model; the genuinely hard part of routing is building the evals that determine which intelligence to use for which application, so eval work is what actually enables router adoption.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Routing layers do not capture value from intelligence allocation unless they own evaluation — a caution on valuing gateway businesses as if they were smart routers, and a reason eval firms sit upstream of them.
insights.quote: the hardest part of routing is building the evals and trying to determine uh in what places a set of intelligences should be used for a particular application

insights.claim: Vals AI built a recursive self-improvement index by constructing proxies for each stage of building a next-generation model — pre-training, post-training, and harness-level engineering — because the ideal test of having a frontier model actually train its own successor is too expensive and slow to run.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, watchable metric for AI-accelerating-AI progress — the input that most changes capex assumptions and timelines if it starts moving fast.
insights.quote: in an ideal world what you want to do is actually take a frontier model and and have it train the next version of itself

insights.claim: Big labs are already discussing recursive self-improvement and starting to report on it in their model cards, but there is no shared language for comparing RSI potential across models — a measurement gap an apples-to-apples third-party index is being built to fill.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: RSI is moving from research talk to disclosed metric — a new comparable that could become the headline number labs are judged on, the way benchmark suites once were.

insights.claim: Recursive self-improvement, not bio or cyber risk, is the most important long-term geopolitical variable, because a single country or company could run away with it and produce models operating in ways unknown to everyone else — which is why researchers at closed-source labs are calling for joint government conversations today.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Frames RSI as the tail risk with the largest asymmetric payoff and the most likely trigger for binding international AI policy — a discontinuity risk for anyone underwriting a multi-lab competitive equilibrium.
insights.quote: you could see one country, one or one company kind of run away with it and produce models that we we don't know much about

insights.claim: Government should set and enforce the rules while a competent private company does the testing, because evaluating capability is a poor long-term government function — and the testing itself is two distinct questions: can the model do the harmful thing, and can someone actually get the model to do it.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz
insights.so_what: Sketches the likely regulatory architecture — a rule-setting state plus a private testing industry — which would make accredited evaluators a compliance-driven, recurring-revenue category.
insights.quote: the government sets and enforces the rules and that um a very competent kind of private company then tells them if the rule is broken

insights.claim: AI policy debate over the last couple of years has been abstract with no material grounding, and even lab proposals for a third-party testing ecosystem never specify the mechanism by which it would work — so Vals AI is in evidence-gathering mode and now regularly briefs both the executive and legislative branches on model capabilities and risks.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Whoever supplies the empirical baseline to policymakers shapes the eventual rules and gets designated as the measurement standard — regulatory capture risk and a durable moat for the incumbent evaluator.
insights.quote: policy conversations as they've happened over the last couple of years have been very abstract

insights.claim: AI needs a nuclear-arms-control-style 'trust but verify' regime: a Xi Jinping-Trump meeting is scheduled for next month, but unlike warhead counts verified by flyovers there is no mechanism to actually verify AI claims, and a shared language of evaluations is what would make cross-border verification possible.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Positions standardized evals as the technical prerequisite for any US-China AI agreement — meaning eval standards, not compute caps, may become the negotiated instrument to watch.
insights.quote: Reagan had this line, trust but verify

insights.claim: From a global-efficiency standpoint the scale of sovereign AI investment is surprising and wasteful — replicating data centers, data engineering and very large training runs that could be consolidated — but that duplication is the direction the world is actually heading, which raises the need for a shared cross-national evaluation framework.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Sovereign AI spend is politically driven rather than economically optimal, which implies more total data-center capex than efficiency logic would justify — bullish for infrastructure suppliers, cautionary on eventual returns.
insights.quote: I'm surprised to see so much investment in sovereign AI

insights.claim: Cybersecurity evaluation is moving beyond code-level vulnerabilities and memory leaks toward simulating entire enterprise cloud and even electrical grid environments, because the largest risks are at the infrastructure level and are not expressed in code at all.
insights.speaker: Ryan (Vals AI co-founder)
insights.so_what: Next-generation AI security evaluation requires expensive simulated environments — a capital and expertise barrier that concentrates the market and creates a distinct sandbox/simulation tooling opportunity.

insights.claim: Large labs are increasingly resolving dangerous-capability findings by withholding the model from everyone and using it internally while trying to stop their own people from misusing it — and even that containment does not always work.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz
insights.so_what: Internal-only frontier capability widens the gap between what labs can do and what customers can buy, concentrating economic advantage inside the labs and creating a hidden-capability risk for competitors and regulators alike.
insights.quote: the model's got the capability and you can get it to do the bad thing so we're not going to let anybody have it we'll just use it
